findings.problem: The stated expected output is wrong/imprecise. By the time `ip_rcv` runs, `eth_type_trans` has already done `skb_pull(skb, ETH_HLEN)`, advancing `data` 14 bytes past `head`. So headroom measured at ip_rcv is NET_SKB_PAD (64) + 14 = ~78, landing in the lhist `[64, 80)` bucket — not '~64 bytes'. Claiming the peak is exactly NET_SKB_PAD hides the very header-advance mechanism (skb_pull moving `data`) the chapter just taught.
findings.evidence: Histogram of headroom on packets entering `ip_rcv`. You'll see most packets have ~64 bytes of headroom (NET_SKB_PAD).
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: 'You'll see most packets land in the [64, 80) bucket — NET_SKB_PAD (64) plus the 14-byte Ethernet header that eth_type_trans already pulled before ip_rcv runs, which advanced `data` and grew the headroom by ETH_HLEN.'

verification.reasoning: At ip_rcv the headroom (data - head) is NET_SKB_PAD plus ETH_HLEN, because eth_type_trans() runs skb_pull_inline(skb, ETH_HLEN) on the RX path before netif_receive_skb -> ip_rcv, advancing data by 14 bytes. So the typical value is ~78 (64+14), not ~64. The book's 'most packets have ~64 bytes of headroom (NET_SKB_PAD)' hides the skb_pull/data-advance mechanism the chapter just taught — a valid minor pedagogy fix. The trace syntax itself is correct: (uint64) casts on the pointer subtraction satisfy bug-pattern #3, args->skb-> is used (not bare skb), and exit() is parenthesized. Note: with lhist(...,0,256,16) both 64 and 78 fall in the same [64,80) bucket, so the displayed bucket label does not change — the imprecision is purely in the prose. Also the absolute headroom can be larger than 64 on drivers using page_pool/XDP/virtio reserve, so 'exactly NET_SKB_PAD' is doubly imprecise. This is not the environment non-firing issue (that concern is orthogonal and not the basis of this finding).
verification.refinedFix: Reword line 125 to teach the pull: "You'll see the peak in the [64, 80) bucket. The exact number can be larger on drivers that reserve extra (page_pool/XDP), but the +14 from the Ethernet pull is the mechanism to notice."

findings.section: Use ftrace to see the call chain
findings.problem: The only packet the reader deterministically generates is `ping -c 1 8.8.8.8`, which is ICMP. An ICMP echo reply is delivered via `ip_local_deliver -> icmp_rcv`. But the stated expected call tree ends `... -> ip_local_deliver -> tcp_v4_rcv`. The reader who generates exactly the prescribed packet will NOT see tcp_v4_rcv as the leaf; they will see icmp_rcv. The documented success output contradicts the documented trigger, so the reader cannot confirm the trace worked.

findings.suggestedFix: Make the expected leaf match the ICMP trigger: end the chain with `-> ip_local_deliver -> icmp_rcv` (and `icmp_reply`/`icmp_echo` for the reply handling). Alternatively, if you want tcp_v4_rcv, change the trigger to a TCP packet, e.g. `curl -s http://example.com >/dev/null` instead of ping, and keep tcp_v4_rcv as the leaf.

findings.section: Use ftrace to see the call chain
findings.problem: The recording window is only `sleep 5`, and the trigger (`ping`) plus the report command are shown as the next blocks. A reader copy-pasting top-to-bottom runs the blocking `trace-cmd record` (5 s), and only afterwards runs `ping` — capturing nothing. The `# In another terminal` comment is buried inside the first fenced block. Also `trace-cmd` is not a default package and `function_graph` requires CONFIG_FUNCTION_GRAPH_TRACER; neither prerequisite is stated. Finally `trace-cmd report | head -100` may truncate before the ping's subtree under 5 s of background netif_receive_skb traffic.

sudo trace-cmd record -p function_graph ... sleep 5

# In another terminal, generate one packet:
ping -c 1 8.8.8.8

findings.section: Inspect the per-CPU RX state / Adjust netdev_budget
findings.problem: The prose says 'Watch softnet_stat shift' after bumping netdev_budget to 600, but on an idle box `time_squeeze` only increments when a softirq actually exhausts its budget under heavy RX load — which never happens at idle, so changing 300->600 produces no observable shift and the observation demonstrates nothing. Additionally the two `echo` lines (set 600, then restore) are contiguous in one fenced block, so a copy-paste reader applies and immediately reverts the value, never observing the box running at 600.
findings.evidence: echo 600 | sudo tee /proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget\n# restore when done\necho "$old_budget" | sudo tee /proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget   ... Watch `softnet_stat` shift
findings.suggestedFix: Split the block: set 600, then add a load generator that can exhaust the budget (e.g. `iperf3 -c <host> -P 16` or a packet flood) while re-reading `/proc/net/softnet_stat` to watch the time_squeeze column, THEN restore. State that on a truly idle host the counters will not move and load is required to see any effect.

verification.reasoning: Both sub-claims are valid against the file. (1) softnet_stat's time_squeeze column (defined line 135 as budget exhaustions) only increments when net_rx_action hits the netdev_budget ceiling under sustained heavy RX; on an idle host raising 300->600 produces no observable change, so the line-146 instruction 'Watch softnet_stat shift' demonstrates nothing. (2) The fenced block (lines 140-143) sets 600 and then immediately restores $old_budget with no observation step between, so a copy-paste reader never runs at 600 — and this also contradicts line 146 which says to watch THEN restore (the block already restored). The commands themselves are syntactically fine (echo|sudo tee to /proc/sys works), so this is a no-expected-output/pedagogy defect, not a broken command, and not the environment non-firing-probe nuance. Severity major is right.
verification.refinedFix: Split the single block into a set step and a separate restore step, with an observation step between, and be honest about what is/isn't visible. Set: `old_budget=$(cat /proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget); echo 600 | sudo tee /proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget`. Then under sustained RX load (e.g. `iperf3 -c <host> -P 16` from another box, or a packet flood) re-read `/proc/net/softnet_stat` repeatedly and watch the 3rd column (time_squeeze) per CPU. Then restore in its own block: `echo "$old_budget" | sudo tee /proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget`. State explicitly that on an idle host time_squeeze never moves — load that actually exhausts the per-softirq budget is required — and warn that even under load time_squeeze can stay flat on fast CPUs / multi-queue NICs, so a non-moving counter is normal rather than a sign the budget change failed. Verify the budget actually changed instead with `cat /proc/sys/net/core/netdev_budget`.

findings.section: Trace a TCP send all the way through
findings.problem: The capture (`trace-cmd record ... sleep 5`) runs for only 5 seconds, and the trigger (`echo hello | nc ... 8.8.8.8 80`) must be pasted into a SECOND terminal within that window. The chapter never states the timing constraint. If the reader is a few seconds slow switching terminals, `sleep 5` ends, the recording stops, and `trace-cmd report` shows no tcp_sendmsg tree at all. The day01 bar (Obs2/Obs3) makes the trigger fire reliably during the capture rather than racing a hand-coordinated second terminal.
findings.evidence: sudo trace-cmd record -p function_graph -g tcp_sendmsg ... sleep 5\n# In another terminal:\necho "hello" | nc -q 1 8.8.8.8 80
findings.suggestedFix:
Run the trigger INSIDE the recorded command so it is guaranteed to fire during capture, eliminating the two-terminal race:

sudo trace-cmd record -p function_graph -g tcp_sendmsg \
    -O nofuncgraph-overhead -O funcgraph-tail \
    bash -c 'echo hello | nc -q1 example.com 80; sleep 1'
sudo trace-cmd report | head -200

verification.reasoning: The capture is `trace-cmd record ... -g tcp_sendmsg sleep 5`, which records only for the 5s lifetime of the `sleep 5` child. The trigger `echo hello | nc -q 1 8.8.8.8 80` lives in a SECOND terminal with no stated timing constraint. A reader who is slow switching terminals misses the window, `sleep 5` exits, recording stops, and `trace-cmd report` shows no tcp_sendmsg tree — the experiment silently produces nothing. This is a genuine hand-coordination race, not an environment-only non-firing probe (the syntax and probe are valid). Embedding the trigger inside the recorded command via `bash -c '...; sleep 1'` makes trace-cmd record for exactly as long as the trigger runs, guaranteeing the call tree is captured. This matches the reliable-trigger pattern used on day01.

findings.section: Trace a TCP send all the way through
findings.problem: The trigger depends on outbound internet reachability to 8.8.8.8:80 and on a specific `nc` implementation. Google's 8.8.8.8 does answer on :80 but a firewalled/offline test VM has no route to it, so the TCP handshake never completes and tcp_sendmsg for the payload never fires. Also `-q 1` is a netcat-openbsd/traditional flag; nmap's `ncat` does not accept it. Neither the internet prerequisite nor the nc variant is stated.
findings.evidence: echo "hello" | nc -q 1 8.8.8.8 80
findings.suggestedFix: State the prerequisite ('needs outbound TCP and a BSD/traditional `nc`; on `ncat` drop `-q1`') or use a host the reader is known to reach, e.g. their default gateway or `example.com 80`. Any completed TCP send works — the only requirement is that the connection actually establishes during the capture window.

verification.reasoning: Line 116 reads `echo \"hello\" | nc -q 1 8.8.8.8 80`. The experiment traces `tcp_sendmsg` (line 110), which only fires when userspace actually writes data over an established connection. `nc` pipes \"hello\" to stdin and sends it only after the TCP handshake completes, so on a firewalled/offline VM with no route to 8.8.8.8 the connection never establishes and the payload send (the thing being traced) never fires — the report would be empty. The internet-reachability prerequisite is genuinely unstated. The `-q` portability claim is also correct: `-q <seconds>` (quit N seconds after EOF) is an OpenBSD/traditional-netcat flag; nmap's `ncat` does not accept `-q` and would error. Neither caveat is mentioned. This is a legitimate missing-setup note, not a bpftrace bug-pattern violation, hence minor severity. Not an environment-quirk false positive: the issue is the book not stating a real prerequisite, not a probe that mysteriously fails to fire.
verification.refinedFix: Add a one-line prerequisite note: this needs outbound TCP reachability and a BSD/traditional `nc` (on nmap's `ncat`, drop `-q 1`). Better, use a host the reader is guaranteed to reach so the handshake reliably completes during the 5s capture, e.g. `echo \"hello\" | nc -w1 example.com 80` (or the default gateway). Any connection that actually establishes triggers `tcp_sendmsg` for the payload; the only hard requirement is a completed handshake inside the capture window.

findings.problem: `ss -tim` on an idle box shows only the reader's SSH session (or nothing), and its wmem_queued/unacked/cwnd values are static and near zero. The whole point of Stage 2 (send buffer fills, sk_wmem_queued caps it) and the chapter's own check question (compare `unacked` vs `wmem_queued`) is invisible without an active bulk transfer. No load/trigger step is given, unlike the day01 standard which always provokes the phenomenon first.
findings.evidence: ss -tim\n\nPer-socket: send buffer used, congestion window, RTO, retransmits. Look at `wmem_*` fields.
findings.suggestedFix:
Add a self-contained transfer before the snapshot, e.g.:

iperf3 -s >/dev/null &            # local sink
iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1 -t 30 &       # sustained send
ss -tim | grep -A1 127.0.0.1      # now wmem_queued / unacked are populated

and tell the reader to watch `wmem_queued` (bytes copied into sk_write_queue) climb while `unacked` (sent-but-not-ACKed) tracks the in-flight window — directly demonstrating Stage 2 and answering the check question. Stop the iperf3 jobs afterward.

verification.reasoning: The 'Watch socket buffer accounting' step (lines 125-129) runs `ss -tim` with no traffic generator, unlike the adjacent experiment steps which provoke the phenomenon first (`nc 8.8.8.8 80` for the trace step; `iperf3` + `tbf` for the backlog step). On an idle box `ss -tim` shows only the SSH control socket with unacked=0 and a tiny static wmem_queued, so Stage 2 (lines 36-38: send buffer fills until sk_wmem_queued caps at sk_sndbuf) is unobservable. The check question (line 187) explicitly sends the reader back to this command to compare `unacked` vs `wmem_queued` — a comparison that yields nothing without an active bulk transfer. So the missing-trigger complaint is real. The command itself is valid (not a broken-command case); this is a genuine wont-fire-or-empty gap, not an environment quirk. Caveat on the auditor's fix: iperf3 over loopback (127.0.0.1) is a weak demonstrator because loopback drains near-instantly with ~0 RTT, keeping wmem_queued/unacked small; a rate-limited or remote path fills the send buffer reliably.
verification.refinedFix:
Add a sustained, bandwidth-constrained transfer before the snapshot so the send buffer actually fills, then watch ss -tim. Reuse the chapter's own tbf limiter rather than loopback (loopback drains too fast to fill sk_wmem_queued):

```bash
# Constrain egress so the send buffer backs up (same tbf the backlog step uses):
sudo tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root tbf rate 1mbit burst 32kbit latency 50ms
iperf3 -c <remote-host> -t 30 &
watch -n1 'ss -tim dst <remote-host>'   # wmem_queued climbs toward sk_sndbuf; unacked = in-flight (cwnd)
# restore afterward:
sudo tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq_codel
```

Tell the reader to watch `wmem_queued` (bytes copied into sk_write_queue) climb toward `sk_sndbuf` while `unacked` (sent-but-not-ACKed) tracks the congestion/receive window — directly demonstrating Stage 2 and answering the check question. If a remote host is unavailable, note that `iperf3 -c 127.0.0.1` populates the fields with non-zero values but won't fully exercise the buffer cap because loopback has no bottleneck.

findings.problem: `iperf3 -c some-target` is a placeholder, not a runnable command — it needs a reachable iperf3 server, and `some-target` is never defined. Worse, the experiment is subtle: tbf on eth0 only rate-limits EGRESS on that device, so the backlog only grows if traffic actually leaves eth0. A localhost iperf3 (127.0.0.1) traverses `lo`, NOT eth0's qdisc, so it would show zero backlog — meaning there is no self-contained substitute. The reader is left with a command that cannot run and a non-obvious reason a naive localhost fix fails.

(Loopback won't work — tbf on eth0 only sees traffic egressing eth0.)' Then sample the backlog repeatedly: `watch -n1 "tc -s qdisc show dev \$IFACE"` so the growing `backlog ... requeues` line is actually visible rather than caught in a single snapshot.

findings.problem: GRO is a RECEIVE-side coalescer, but the suggested trigger generates the wrong traffic direction. `iperf3 -c <server>` (default/forward) sends data OUT of this host; the inbound traffic is mostly small ACKs, so GRO has almost nothing to coalesce and `gro_receive_skb`/`ip_rcv` will not show the big coalesced superpackets the section promises. findings.problem: `ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i tx_pkts` produces no output (verified: exit status 1, empty) on real NICs. No driver names a stat 'tx_pkts'; the actual counters are 'tx_queue_N_packets', 'vf_tx_packets', 'cpuN_tx_packets', plus the kernel's /sys statistics. The substring 'tx_pkts' never matches 'tx_packets'. The observation also gives no load/trigger step (idle box's TX barely moves) and no concrete expected numbers, and never shows how to obtain the kernel skb count for the `wire_pkts >> tx_packets_kernel` comparison it describes.

State the expected result: NIC wire count >> kernel skb count when TSO is active.

verification.reasoning: Line 143's `ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i tx_pkts` is broken/fragile: `tx_pkts` is not a substring of `tx_packets`, the field name nearly all NICs actually expose (mlx5, Intel, hv_netvsc on Azure, virtio_net all use `tx_packets`/`tx_queue_N_packets`). Only a handful of drivers (e.g. be2net) literally use `tx_pkts`, so on the generic `eth0` the chapter assumes, the grep commonly prints nothing — consistent with the verified empty/exit-1 result. Additionally the section gives no load step (idle TX barely moves) and describes a `wire_pkts >> tx_packets_kernel` ratio without ever showing how to read the kernel-side count, so the reader can't perform the comparison. verification.refinedFix:
Replace the fragile grep with a portable field match and show both sides of the ratio under load. e.g.:

  # generate TX load first (large upload), e.g. iperf3 -c SERVER  or  curl -T bigfile https://SERVER/
  ethtool -S eth0 | grep -iE 'tx_packets|tx_queue.*packets'   # NIC's reported packet counts
  cat /sys/class/net/eth0/statistics/tx_packets               # kernel-level tx_packets

Expected: with TSO active, the count of large skbs the stack handed down is far smaller than the wire segments the NIC actually transmitted. Note that on many drivers /sys statistics/tx_packets is itself populated from the driver and may already reflect wire packets, so the cleanest "stack vs wire" demonstration is to compare the byte/packet rate against MTU, or to use a bpftrace count on the relevant TX skb path; at minimum, use the real `tx_packets`-family field names rather than the non-matching `tx_pkts`.

findings.problem: `sudo ip netns exec green readlink /proc/$$/ns/net` does NOT read green's namespace. `$$` is expanded by the outer interactive shell (which lives in init_net) before `ip netns exec` ever runs, so readlink resolves the symlink for the OUTER shell's PID — a process still in init_net. The result is identical to the first readlink, so the stated payoff 'The two readlinks differ' is false as written; the reader sees two identical inodes and the observation fails to demonstrate anything.
findings.evidence: sudo ip netns exec green readlink /proc/$$/ns/net   # then prose: "The two readlinks differ"
findings.suggestedFix: Use /proc/self inside the exec so the symlink is resolved by the readlink process that `ip netns exec` actually placed in green: `sudo ip netns exec green readlink /proc/self/ns/net`. Keep the first command as `readlink /proc/$$/ns/net` (current shell = init_net). The two inodes will then genuinely differ.

verification.reasoning: At line 106, `$$` is expanded by the outer interactive shell (in init_net) before `ip netns exec` runs, so it equals the OUTER shell's PID. `ip netns exec green` moves only the spawned readlink into green, but the path /proc/<outer-PID>/ns/net still references the outer shell, which stays in init_net; /proc shows the same PID->namespace mapping regardless. So line 106 resolves to the same init_net inode as line 105, making the line-109 claim 'The two readlinks differ' false. The fix to use /proc/self is correct: with `ip netns exec green readlink /proc/self/ns/net`, 'self' is the readlink process itself, which was placed in green, so it resolves to green's net namespace inode and genuinely differs.

The example also assumes `bbr` is the running value without verifying it is even compiled in.

The header's 'bbr (or whatever)' hedge does not save it, because the trailing comments and prose are written as definite expected output and the chosen value (cubic) is precisely the common default. Using reno — always built into the kernel as the fallback — guarantees a value distinct from init's. This is determinable from the file plus standard kernel defaults; no run needed. findings.problem: The fallback hint says to 'trace the creation path via copy_net_ns ... which has a struct net * once setup_net returns'. This misleads: copy_net_ns's signature is copy_net_ns(unsigned long flags, struct user_namespace *user_ns, struct net *old_net) — its struct net arg (args->old_net) is the OLD namespace, not the new one. The new net is the RETURN value, so a reader who tries `fentry:copy_net_ns { args->net }` gets an Unknown-identifier error.

findings.section: What to break — Try moving a physical NIC to a netns
findings.problem: The command hardcodes `eth0`, but many cloud/test VMs use predictable names (ens5, enp0s3, etc.), so the literal command fails with 'Cannot find device'. The recovery snippet also implies SSH returns automatically, but after moving the NIC back to init_net it is administratively down with no addresses — connectivity needs an explicit up + re-DHCP.
findings.evidence:
sudo ip link set eth0 netns red    # **CAREFUL**
...
sudo ip netns exec red ip link set eth0 netns 1   # back to init_net
findings.suggestedFix: Tell the reader to discover their interface first: `ip route get 1.1.1.1` (the `dev <name>` field) and substitute it for eth0. In the recovery block add: `sudo ip link set eth0 up && sudo dhclient eth0` (or re-add the static address) after moving it back, since the interface comes back down and address-less.

verification.reasoning: Two claims. (1) Hardcoded eth0: partially mitigated already — the book warns at line 191 to use 'a non-essential interface or via a console,' and eth0 is clearly illustrative, not a reproducible lab step. So the 'Cannot find device' complaint is weakened but a discovery hint is still a fair improvement. (2) Recovery incompleteness: this is a real, kernel-accurate defect. Moving a netdev into another netns flushes its IPv4 addresses and leaves the link administratively DOWN; moving it back (line 195) returns it to init_net still down and address-less. The recovery snippet alone does NOT restore connectivity, so the section's implied 'move it back to recover' is incomplete. Not a bpftrace/CLI syntax issue and not the environment-non-firing nuance. Severity minor is appropriate.
verification.refinedFix:
Keep the existing CAREFUL/console warning. In the recovery block, after moving the device back to init_net, add the steps needed to actually restore connectivity, since the device returns DOWN with its addresses flushed:

sudo ip netns exec red ip link set eth0 netns 1   # back to init_net
sudo ip link set eth0 up
sudo dhclient eth0        # or re-add the static address you had before

Optionally, as a secondary improvement, tell the reader to discover their real interface name first (predictable names like ens5/enp0s3 are common) with `ip route get 1.1.1.1` and read the `dev <name>` field, substituting it for eth0.

findings.problem: bpftrace is backgrounded with '&' and then 'ping -c 1 8.8.8.8' fires immediately, followed instantly by 'sudo killall bpftrace'. The gold standard always lets the probe attach before generating the trigger.

findings.problem: Changing the MAC of eth0 is presented with no safety warning and no cleanup. On the SSH-accessed test VM, eth0 is the management interface — changing its MAC drops the link layer / DHCP lease and kills the SSH session, and there is no step to restore the original address. Many drivers also reject an address change while the link is up. There is likewise no command to observe the result.

findings.suggestedFix:
Warn, save the original, bring the link down/up, observe, and restore:

# link and your connection. Prefer a spare/veth interface. Save the original first:
orig=$(cat /sys/class/net/eth0/address)
sudo ip link set eth0 down
sudo ip link set eth0 address 02:00:00:00:00:01
sudo ip link set eth0 up
# re-run the eth_type_trans trace: frames to 02:00:00:00:00:01 are now PACKET_HOST.
sudo ip link set eth0 down
sudo ip link set eth0 address "$orig"
sudo ip link set eth0 up

verification.reasoning: Lines 125-129 give `sudo ip link set eth0 address 02:00:00:00:00:01` with zero safety context: no warning, no saved original, no restore, and no observation step. On the SSH-accessed test VM (per MEMORY, kernel 7.0 reached over SSH), eth0 is the management interface, so changing its MAC drops the link-layer identity / DHCP lease and can sever the session — leaving the reader locked out with no documented way back. This is a genuine book defect, not a bpftrace/CLI syntax issue and not the Azure non-firing-probe environment quirk. Note the auditor's own fix has a subtlety: `ip link set eth0 down` on the management interface ALSO kills SSH, so the real mitigation is the warning to run this on a spare/veth/dummy interface rather than the down/up dance on eth0. The down/up is still useful because some drivers reject a MAC change while the link is up. I mark confidence medium rather than high only because the severity hinges on eth0 being the SSH path (true for this VM) and because "many drivers reject the change while up" varies by driver (virtio/hv_netvsc often allow it).

findings.problem: Two problems. (1) 'ping 192.168.1.1' has no -c count, so it runs until the reader manually Ctrl-Cs; the 'undo' (ip neigh del) line never executes on its own, leaving the gateway ARP poisoned. (2) Poisoning the gateway's MAC kills connectivity through that gateway. A reader SSH'd into the box over that very interface loses the session at the ping step and can no longer run the 'del' to recover — a self-lockout. There is no warning about this.
findings.evidence:
sudo ip neigh add 192.168.1.1 lladdr aa:bb:cc:00:00:00 dev eth0 nud permanent
ping 192.168.1.1   # times out — packets sent to wrong MAC

# undo:
sudo ip neigh del 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
findings.suggestedFix: Bound the ping and warn about remote sessions: change to 'ping -c 3 -W 1 192.168.1.1   # times out — packets sent to wrong MAC' and add a callout: 'Do NOT do this on the interface you are SSH-ing in over — poisoning the gateway MAC drops your session before you can run the undo. Pin a non-gateway peer instead, or run it from the console.' Better still, pin a harmless test peer rather than the default gateway.

verification.reasoning: Lines 116-122 show `sudo ip neigh add 192.168.1.1 lladdr aa:bb:cc:00:00:00 dev eth0 nud permanent` / `ping 192.168.1.1   # times out` / undo `ip neigh del`. Both sub-claims hold. (1) The ping has no `-c`, so it runs forever; against a wrong-MAC destination there are simply no replies, so ping never actually exits — the `# times out` comment is inaccurate and the `# undo:` `ip neigh del` line is never reached unless the reader manually Ctrl-Cs. (2) 192.168.1.1 is the canonical gateway address, explicitly chosen here; pinning a bogus MAC as `nud permanent` poisons the gateway entry and severs all traffic routed through it. A reader connected over eth0 via SSH loses the session at the ping step and can no longer issue the `del` to recover — a self-lockout with no warning in the text. The commands are syntactically valid (no bpftrace/CLI bug-pattern issue), so this is a safety/ergonomics defect, not a broken-command one; "critical" is slightly strong but the lockout risk is genuine.

findings.problem: Two correctness issues. (1) 10.99.99.99 is off-subnet for the chapter's own 192.168.1.0/24 example network, so a packet to it is routed via the default gateway and the kernel never ARPs for 10.99.99.99 — the manually added entry on eth0 is never exercised. (2) 'ip neigh add' without sending any traffic does not necessarily kick off resolution; an entry sitting idle won't march INCOMPLETE->FAILED on its own. So 'sleep 5; ip neigh show' commonly shows a static/incomplete entry, not the promised FAILED. The hedged comment 'INCOMPLETE / FAILED after retries' signals the author already noticed it is unreliable. Missing cleanup too: the 10.99.99.99 entry is never deleted, unlike the wrong-MAC section.
findings.evidence:
sudo ip neigh add 10.99.99.99 dev eth0   # nonexistent host
sleep 5
ip neigh show 10.99.99.99
# 10.99.99.99 dev eth0 INCOMPLETE / FAILED after retries
findings.suggestedFix:
Pick an UNUSED address inside your own subnet and drive resolution with traffic, then clean up:
```bash
# pick an unused IP in your eth0 subnet, e.g. 192.168.1.250
sudo ip neigh flush 192.168.1.250 dev eth0 2>/dev/null
ping -c1 -W1 192.168.1.250 || true   # kicks off ARP resolution
sleep 8                                # > 3 multicast probes @ retrans_time 1s
ip neigh show 192.168.1.250
# 192.168.1.250 dev eth0  FAILED
sudo ip neigh del 192.168.1.250 dev eth0   # cleanup
```

verification.reasoning: The demo does not reliably produce the promised FAILED state. (1) iproute2 defaults a no-nud/no-lladdr `ip neigh add` to NUD_PERMANENT, creating a static entry that the kernel never probes — so it cannot reach FAILED. (2) The NUD state machine is driven by the output path (a queued skb / neigh_event_send), not by inserting a netlink entry; with zero traffic the multicast-solicit retransmit cycle is never armed, so an idle entry does not progress to FAILED. (3) 10.99.99.99 is off-subnet for the chapter's 192.168.1.0/24, so any traffic would route via the gateway and never ARP the target — making it the wrong address to demonstrate ARP failure on eth0. The book's own hedge "INCOMPLETE / FAILED after retries" reflects the nondeterminism, and there is no cleanup `ip neigh del` (inconsistent with the wrong-MAC section directly above). The suggested fix correctly uses an unused in-subnet IP plus a ping to drive ARP, waits past the multicast probes, and cleans up. Confidence medium because SSH to the test VM was blocked, so this is from iproute2/kernel behavior rather than a live run.
verification.refinedFix:
Drive resolution with real traffic to an UNUSED address inside your eth0 subnet, then clean up. Replace 192.168.1.250 with an address you know is unused on your link:

```bash
sudo ip neigh flush 192.168.1.250 dev eth0 2>/dev/null
ping -c1 -W1 192.168.1.250 || true   # queues a packet -> kernel starts ARPing
sleep 8                               # past 3 multicast probes @ retrans_time 1s
ip neigh show 192.168.1.250
# 192.168.1.250 dev eth0  FAILED      (briefly INCOMPLETE first)
sudo ip neigh del 192.168.1.250 dev eth0   # cleanup
```

Note in the prose that a bare `ip neigh add IP dev eth0` (no lladdr/nud) creates a static PERMANENT entry that never probes — to watch the FAILED transition you must send traffic to an unused, directly-connected IP.

findings.section: What to break — Break a default route safely, inside a namespace
findings.problem: The route-add command fails as written, so the entire experiment never demonstrates its point. `sudo ip -n fibbreak route add default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo` returns `Error: Nexthop has invalid gateway.` (exit 2) because 10.99.99.99 is not on any subnet configured on lo (lo carries only 127.0.0.1/8). Because the route is never installed, the subsequent ping fails with `connect: Network is unreachable` (there is NO default route at all) — not because 'the lookup succeeds but transmission cannot resolve a usable path' as the prose claims. The prose explanation at line 158 is therefore describing behavior that never happens.
findings.evidence: sudo ip -n fibbreak route add default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo   ->  Error: Nexthop has invalid gateway. (exit 2); ping then -> ping: connect: Network is unreachable
findings.suggestedFix: Add the `onlink` flag so the kernel accepts the off-subnet gateway: `sudo ip -n fibbreak route add default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo onlink`. Verified on the 7.0 VM: the route then installs (`default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo onlink`) and the ping yields '100% packet loss' (exit 1) — exactly the intended 'lookup succeeds, transmission cannot resolve a usable path.' Alternatively give the namespace a dummy device with an address in the gateway's subnet first.

verification.reasoning: Line 152's `ip route add default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo` is rejected by the kernel's FIB nexthop validation (fib_check_nh) with `Error: Nexthop has invalid gateway.` because 10.99.99.99 is off-subnet for lo (which only carries 127.0.0.1/8) and the gateway must be directly reachable on the named device unless `onlink` is set. This is documented iproute2/kernel behavior, not an environment-specific quirk. Since the route never installs, the ping fails with `Network is unreachable` (no default route at all), which contradicts the prose at line 158 claiming the lookup succeeds but transmission cannot resolve a path — that scenario requires the route to actually be present. The defect breaks the entire pedagogical point of the experiment.
verification.refinedFix: Add the `onlink` flag so the kernel accepts the off-subnet gateway: `sudo ip -n fibbreak route add default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo onlink`. With this, the route installs (`default via 10.99.99.99 dev lo onlink`), the FIB lookup succeeds, and the ping yields 100% packet loss (exit 1) — matching the prose at line 158. (Alternatively, add a dummy device with an address in the gateway's subnet to the namespace first.) Consider also tweaking the comment on line 153 and prose so the demonstrated failure mode is internally consistent.

Then add a matching `sudo ip addr del 10.99.0.5/32 dev lo 2>/dev/null || true` line to the cleanup() function so the trap removes it.

verification.reasoning: The experiment adds only a route (`ip route add 10.99.0.0/24 dev lo`) but never assigns 10.99.0.5 to any interface. `ping -I 10.99.0.5` (an IP, not an interface name) binds the ICMP socket to that source address; bind() to a non-local address returns EADDRNOTAVAIL (`ping: bind: Cannot assign requested address`). The bind fails before any packet is sent, so no fib lookup runs and `table_id=99` is never printed — contradicting the stated result on line 178. A route on lo does not create the RTN_LOCAL entry needed for binding; only `ip addr add` does. This is a genuine missing-setup defect, runtime-verifiable, not an environment quirk and not a probe-firing issue. The second ping and the bpftrace probes are otherwise fine.
verification.refinedFix: In setup, before the route lines, assign the address: `sudo ip addr add 10.99.0.5/32 dev lo`. The existing `ip route add 10.99.0.0/24 dev lo` may stay or be dropped (the /32 addr installs its own local route). Add a matching cleanup line to the cleanup() function: `sudo ip addr del 10.99.0.5/32 dev lo 2>/dev/null || true` so the EXIT trap removes it. With the address present, the first ping's source is a valid local address, the `from 10.99.0.0/24 lookup 99` rule matches, and `table_id=99` is printed as claimed.

The audit's fix (`sudo ip addr add 10.99.0.5/32 dev lo` before the route lines, plus matching `ip addr del` in cleanup) is correct and produces the promised `table_id=99`. findings.problem: bpftrace is launched in the background with `&` and the two pings run immediately afterward with no pause. fentry probe attachment takes a noticeable fraction of a second (BTF load + attach); the first `ping -c 1` (a single packet) can easily complete its route lookup before `fib_table_lookup` is attached, so `table_id=99` is missed and the reader sees empty/partial output. day01 sidesteps this by using interval-driven traces that run for 5s; a single one-shot ping has no such margin.
findings.evidence:
sudo bpftrace -e '...' &
tracer=$!

# Send packet from 10.99 source
ping -I 10.99.0.5 -c 1 8.8.8.8
findings.suggestedFix: Insert `sleep 2` after `tracer=$!` (and before the first ping) to let the fentry probes attach, e.g. add a line `sleep 2   # let bpftrace attach its probes before we send traffic`.

verification.reasoning: The bpftrace syntax is valid (args->tb->tb_id, count() are correct — no bug-pattern violation). The real issue is the attach race: bpftrace is backgrounded with `&` and `ping -I 10.99.0.5 -c 1 8.8.8.8` runs with zero pause. fentry attach (codegen + vmlinux BTF load + link create) takes ~0.5–3s, while ping's first-packet route lookup fires within milliseconds, so the first lookup very likely happens before fib_table_lookup is attached — and `table_id=99` (the headline result on line 178) is missed. This experiment is uniquely race-sensitive compared to the otherwise-identical backgrounded patterns in day06 (eth_type_trans) and day20 (nf_hook_slow): those probes fire on continuous background traffic that masks a late attach, whereas fib_table_lookup only fires on the two specific, uncached route lookups this lab deliberately triggers, and `-c 1` caches the route so there is no later lookup to catch. The second ping runs only after the first ping exits (seconds later), so table_id=254 would still appear — exactly matching the asymmetric failure (reader sees 254 but not 99). This is a genuine missing pause, not the environment-only non-firing-probe quirk. Confidence is medium rather than high only because the precise attach-vs-send timing can vary with a warm BTF cache; on a slow/cold first run it will reliably miss.
verification.refinedFix: Insert a pause after `tracer=$!` (line 167) and before the first ping so the fentry probes finish attaching, e.g. `sleep 2   # let bpftrace attach its fentry probes before sending traffic`. On a cold/slow box `sleep 3` is safer; the most robust variant is to wait until bpftrace prints "Attaching 2 probes..." This matches the existing book convention (day10 already uses `sleep 1` between attach and trigger).

findings.problem: The stated expected output is incomplete and will confuse the reader. fib_rules walks rule 0 (local, table 255) FIRST for every lookup, and local-table misses also go through fib_table_lookup. So the first ping prints `table_id=255` (local miss) THEN `table_id=99`, and the second ping prints `table_id=255` THEN `table_id=254`. The reader will see extra `table_id=255` lines the prose never mentions and may think the experiment is misbehaving.
findings.evidence: You'll see `table_id=99` for the first ping and `table_id=254` (main) for the second.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to set the real expectation, e.g.: "For each ping you'll first see `table_id=255` (the always-first `local` table lookup, which misses for an external destination). The first ping then shows `table_id=99` — proof the `from 10.99.0.0/24` rule steered it into table 99 — while the second ping falls through to `table_id=254` (main)."

verification.reasoning: The probe fentry:fib_table_lookup fires once per fib_table_lookup call. Because the experiment installs a custom ip rule, net->ipv4.fib_has_custom_rules becomes true, forcing every lookup through fib_rules_lookup, which walks rules in priority order. The built-in local rule (priority 0, table 255) is walked first; its FR_ACT_TO_TBL action calls fib_table_lookup on table 255, which misses for 8.8.8.8 and continues. Only afterward does the priority-99 rule (first ping) or the main rule (second ping) run. So the trace prints table_id=255 BEFORE table_id=99 and again before table_id=254. Line 178 mentions only 99 and 254, so the reader does see unexplained 255 lines — the expected output is genuinely incomplete. Deterministic from kernel source; not an environment quirk. (There may even be more than one 255 line per ping if multiple route lookups occur.)
verification.refinedFix: Reword line 178 to set the real expectation, e.g.: "For each ping you'll first see one or more `table_id=255` lines — that's the always-first `local` table lookup, which misses for an external destination like 8.8.8.8. The first ping then shows `table_id=99`, proof the `from 10.99.0.0/24` rule steered it into table 99; the second ping falls through to `table_id=254` (main)." Mentioning that 255 may repeat avoids confusion if the kernel does multiple lookups per ping.

findings.section: Today's experiment — Watch DAD on bring-up
findings.problem: The bpftrace for ndisc_send_ns is launched in the background with '&' and then 'ip link set eth0 down ... up' is run immediately on the next line. bpftrace needs several seconds to compile the program, load BTF, and attach the fentry probe. The DAD Neighbor Solicitation fired by the link bring-up almost always happens before the probe is attached, so the reader sees nothing — the textbook attach race that day01 avoids by never racing a trigger against a just-backgrounded tracer.
findings.evidence:
sudo bpftrace -e 'fentry:ndisc_send_ns { ... }' &
sudo ip link set eth0 down && sleep 1 && sudo ip link set eth0 up
findings.suggestedFix: Insert a wait for the probe to attach before triggering, e.g.: 'sudo bpftrace -e '...' & sleep 3   # let the probe attach' then run the 'ip link set eth0 down && sleep 1 && sudo ip link set eth0 up' line.

verification.reasoning: The bpftrace fentry:ndisc_send_ns probe is backgrounded with '&', then 'ip link set eth0 down && sleep 1 && sudo ip link set eth0 up' runs immediately. The DAD NS is fired by the 'up', which occurs only ~1s after launch. fentry attach (BTF load + verification + attach) commonly takes several seconds on first run, so the NS very likely fires before the probe attaches and the reader sees no output. This is a real attach race (a missing-setup defect), not an environment-only non-firing probe: the probe target ndisc_send_ns does fire on bring-up and the bpftrace syntax is correct (ntop(args->solicit->in6_u.u6_addr8) follows the proper IPv6 idiom, no bare-field or %pI6 violations). The same race-avoidance discipline is used elsewhere in the book.

findings.vmNotes: Cannot empirically observe the race: the book's trigger downs eth0 (the SSH NIC) — disconnecting and disruptive, disallowed in read-only phase. On the timing the audit's premise is overstated for this VM: attach is ~0.9s (not "several seconds"), and the book's command interposes `sleep 1` before the NS-generating `up`, so the probe is very likely (marginally) attached when the NS fires. The race is real but thin (~0.9s attach vs ~1s margin), not "almost always missed" as claimed. The audit's fix (sleep 3 between backgrounding and trigger) is correct, strictly safer defensive practice and worth adopting — but the defect as worded ("reader sees nothing") is not clearly supported here. Marking inconclusive because the destructive trigger is unrunnable on this box; if reproducing on a non-SSH NIC, the right framing is "tighten the marginal sleep," not "guaranteed attach miss."

The background NS tracer keeps printing into the terminal, interleaving with that output, and stays attached to the kernel after the section ends. The precedent claim checks out: day01 (line 156 'sudo tcpdump ... &', line 172 'sudo pkill tcpdump') backgrounds a privileged tool and explicitly cleans it up, so day10 is inconsistent. This is a legitimate hygiene/quality gap rather than a correctness/syntax bug, hence medium confidence on severity but the problem is real as stated.

findings.section: Today's experiment — Watch DAD on bring-up
findings.problem: 'ip link set eth0 down' is destructive: if the reader is working over SSH and eth0 is the management interface (the common case on the book's SSH test VM), this drops the connection and the subsequent '&& ... up' never runs because the session is gone. No warning is given. day01's pitfall standard requires calling out non-obvious gotchas like this.
findings.evidence: sudo ip link set eth0 down && sleep 1 && sudo ip link set eth0 up
findings.suggestedFix: Add a warning sentence: 'WARNING: do not run this on the interface carrying your SSH session — bringing eth0 down disconnects you and the bring-up never executes. Use a spare/secondary interface, or run it from the VM console, substituting its name for eth0.'

verification.reasoning: Line 135 runs `sudo ip link set eth0 down && sleep 1 && sudo ip link set eth0 up`. On the book's SSH test VM, eth0 is the management interface. Bringing it down drops the SSH connection; the dying session sends SIGHUP to the shell, killing the command chain before the `&& ... up` executes, so the host stays unreachable. This is a genuine, non-obvious footgun with no warning given — consistent with a missing-setup/safety gap, not an environment quirk or a bpftrace syntax issue. The two bpftrace probes in this block (ntop(args->solicit->in6_u.u6_addr8), *args->nexthdrp) are syntactically correct, so the only defect is the missing warning.
verification.refinedFix: Add a warning before the bring-up command: "WARNING: do not run this on the interface carrying your SSH session. Bringing eth0 down drops the connection, and because the shell is killed (SIGHUP) the `&& ... up` never runs, leaving the host unreachable. Either run it from the VM console, or substitute a spare/secondary interface name for eth0." Optionally also suggest a self-restoring form that survives session loss, e.g. `sudo nohup sh -c 'ip link set eth0 down; sleep 1; ip link set eth0 up' &` run on the console — but the primary fix is the explicit warning to use a non-management interface.

findings.section: Today's experiment — Watch NDP traffic globally
findings.problem: On a likely-idle box this tcpdump prints nothing for a long time: NDP NS/NA only occur on neighbor activity, RAs default to ~200 s apart (and only if a router is present), and 'not host ::' explicitly filters out the DAD traffic the previous step generated. There is no trigger step to provoke ICMPv6, no expected-output description, and no time bound or stop instruction (it runs until Ctrl-C). day01 Obs3 provides a trigger (curl loop) before observing.
findings.evidence: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp6 and not host ::
findings.suggestedFix: Bound it and add a trigger, e.g.: 'sudo timeout 10 tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp6 &' then in another shell 'ping6 -c3 ff02::1%eth0   # all-nodes multicast: provokes NA replies' and 'ping6 -c3 <a-neighbor-global-or-LL-addr>   # provokes NS/NA'. State the expected output: 'You should see ICMP6 neighbor solicitation / neighbor advertisement (and possibly router advertisement) lines.' Consider dropping the 'and not host ::' filter (or explain it) so DAD is not silently excluded.

verification.reasoning: The tcpdump command itself is syntactically valid (no bpftrace/CLI bug-pattern violation), so this is not a correctness defect. However the 'wont-fire-or-empty' concern is real: this is a 'watch' command with no in-band trigger, no time bound (runs until Ctrl-C), and no expected-output description. The interface bounce on line 135 does generate NDP, but it executes BEFORE tcpdump attaches and its DAD packets (source ::) are explicitly excluded by 'not host ::', so on an idle/router-less box (e.g. the documented Azure test VM where RAs may never arrive) this can print nothing for a long time. That is a genuine pedagogical gap. The finding is overstated as 'major' (the command works; many real LANs do emit RAs/MLD) and its suggestion to drop 'not host ::' is wrong — that filter is intentional, excluding the DAD traffic the prior bpftrace step already covered. Refined fix keeps the filter, adds a trigger, a time bound, and an expected-output line.
verification.refinedFix: Bound the capture and add an explicit trigger so the step is not silent. E.g.: run `sudo timeout 10 tcpdump -i eth0 -nn icmp6 and not host ::` and, in another shell, `ping -6 -c3 ff02::1%eth0   # all-nodes multicast: every IPv6 host on the link replies` and `ping -6 -c3 <a-LL-or-global-neighbor>   # forces NS/NA address resolution`. Add an expected-output note: "You should see ICMP6 neighbor solicitation / neighbor advertisement lines (and, if a router is present, router solicitation / router advertisement)." Keep `and not host ::` but explain it: it excludes the DAD traffic (source `::`) you already watched in the previous step, so you see steady-state NDP instead. Do NOT drop the filter as the original suggestion proposed. Note that reordering also helps: start tcpdump BEFORE the `ip link ... up` bounce if you want to catch the bring-up NDP burst.

findings.vmNotes: Defect is real: on the idle VM the step is completely silent — no neighbor activity, no router present (so no RAs), and `not host ::` filters out the DAD traffic generated by the preceding link down/up step. The book provides no trigger, no expected output, and no stop/time bound. The audit's fix is sound; the `ping -6 ff02::1%eth0` trigger reliably yields ICMPv6 lines. One nuance: the captured frames here are echo request/reply (from the ping itself) rather than the NS/NA the fix text promises — on this single-host link with no unresolved neighbors, multicast echo is what fires. To actually force NS/NA you'd ping an unresolved on-link neighbor address; a lone box may still not show NS/NA. So the fix's broader point (add a trigger + bound + expected-output note) is correct, but its claimed "NS/NA" output is only guaranteed when a real neighbor needing resolution exists.

findings.problem: This bpftrace has no interval/exit and no '&', so it blocks until Ctrl-C, and on an idle box with no IPv6 traffic ipv6_skip_exthdr never fires — the reader stares at a blank screen with no trigger, no expected output, and no clean way to end it (and no exit() to flush). findings.section: Today's experiment — VLAN filtering / flush FDB
findings.problem: `sudo bridge fdb flush dev v1p` (and the v2p variant) FAILS on a real kernel. Without a scope keyword the flush targets the device's own (self/offloaded) FDB, which a veth port does not support, so the kernel returns an error and nothing is flushed. The whole point of this block ('After flushing FDB, traffic should still pass') is silently undermined because the flush never happens.
findings.evidence: sudo bridge fdb flush dev v1p  =>  RTNETLINK answers: Operation not supported  (iproute2/bridge 6.19.0, kernel 7.0)
findings.suggestedFix: Append the `master` scope so it flushes the bridge-learned dynamic entries: `sudo bridge fdb flush dev v1p master` and `sudo bridge fdb flush dev v2p master`. Verified: these succeed and remove the learned dynamic MACs.

verification.reasoning: Verified against iproute2 and kernel source. iproute2 bridge/fdb.c fdb_flush() (lines 849-850) defaults ndm_flags to NTF_SELF when no scope keyword is given. In the kernel rtnl_fdb_del path (net/core/rtnetlink.c v6.12, unchanged in 7.0), the master/bridge branch (line 4461) only fires when ndm_flags is 0 or NTF_MASTER; with NTF_SELF set it instead takes the self branch (line 4481), where the bulk-delete sets err=-EOPNOTSUPP and only clears it if the device itself implements ndo_fdb_del_bulk. A veth port does not, so the kernel returns -EOPNOTSUPP ("Operation not supported"). Thus `sudo bridge fdb flush dev v1p` errors out and flushes nothing, exactly as the finding states. Appending `master` makes iproute2 set NTF_MASTER only, so the kernel dispatches to the bridge's ndo_fdb_del_bulk (br_fdb_delete_bulk) and succeeds. The finding's mechanism explanation is slightly imprecise (the NTF_SELF default comes from iproute2, not from the kernel treating "no scope" as self), but the broken-command claim and the fix are both correct. Could not run live (SSH to test VM was blocked by sandbox), but the source chain is unambiguous.
verification.refinedFix:
Append the `master` scope so the flush targets the bridge-learned dynamic FDB entries instead of the veth's own (unsupported) FDB:
`sudo bridge fdb flush dev v1p master`
`sudo bridge fdb flush dev v2p master`
Rationale to add in prose: without a scope keyword, iproute2 defaults to `self`, and a veth port has no self FDB delete handler, so the kernel returns "Operation not supported" and nothing is flushed; `master` flushes the entries the bridge learned on that port.

findings.section: Inspect the FDB — trace updates (br_fdb_update bpftrace)
findings.problem: The stated expected output is wrong. The prose says 'You'll see one update per src MAC per port; subsequent traffic doesn't refresh until aging.' In reality br_fdb_update is on the per-frame learning hot path and the fentry fires on EVERY received frame, not once per MAC. A 3-packet ping produces three 'learn vid=0 port=v1p' lines (and three for v2p). The reader will see a steady stream and conclude the trace is broken or that the book is wrong.
findings.evidence: Running the exact probe while doing `ping -c 3` printed: 'learn vid=0 port=v1p' / 'learn vid=0 port=v2p' THREE times each — once per frame, not once per MAC.
findings.suggestedFix: Either correct the prose to 'br_fdb_update runs on every received frame (it refreshes the entry's timestamp), so you'll see one line per packet per source port' OR change the probe to aggregate and only show distinct learns, e.g. `fentry:br_fdb_update { @[args->source->dev->name, args->vid] = count(); } interval:s:5 { exit(); }`. Also note vid=0 appears while vlan_filtering is off (it becomes 100 once filtering is enabled).

verification.reasoning: The probe syntax (fentry:br_fdb_update with args->vid, args->source->dev->name) is correct for bpftrace v0.25 — no bug-pattern violation. But the expected-output prose at line 134 is wrong. br_fdb_update is called from br_handle_frame_finish on EVERY received data frame when BR_LEARNING is set (default), as the book itself notes at lines 164/168 ('the per-frame hot path', 'the learning path'). The fentry fires unconditionally on each call, so the printf emits one line per frame, not 'one update per src MAC per port.' A ping -c 2 produces several lines per port (ICMP requests on v1p, replies on v2p, plus ARP). The claim 'subsequent traffic doesn't refresh until aging' is also backwards — active traffic refreshes the entry's updated timestamp (rate-limited to jiffy granularity), which is precisely what keeps entries from aging out. Additionally, since this probe runs before vlan_filtering is enabled at line 138, vid=0 prints (not 100), matching the auditor's note. This is a genuine documentation-accuracy defect, not an environment quirk.
verification.refinedFix: Correct the prose at line 134. br_fdb_update runs on the per-frame learning path, so the probe prints one line per received frame per source port (not once per MAC), and active traffic continuously refreshes the entry's timestamp (that refresh is what prevents aging). Replace line 134 with something like: "br_fdb_update runs on every received frame on the learning path, so you'll see one line per packet per source port; each call refreshes the entry's `updated` timestamp, which is how active entries avoid aging out." findings.section: What to break — Enable br_netfilter + iptables DROP
findings.problem: Underspecified to the point of being non-runnable: no actual iptables rule is given ('add an iptables DROP rule'), no way to observe the effect, and the stated cleanup `iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT` doesn't match any specified rule (it resets the chain policy, not a `-A` rule). It also omits that br_netfilter only invokes iptables when `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1` (set automatically on modprobe) and that the rule must match bridged forwarding.
findings.evidence: Line 157: 'Enable br_netfilter and add an iptables DROP rule on the bridge. ... Disable: `sudo iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT`' — no concrete rule, no observation, mismatched cleanup.
findings.suggestedFix: Give concrete commands: `sudo modprobe br_netfilter`; `sudo sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1`; `sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i br0 -j DROP`; then `sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c2 -W1 10.0.0.2` (now fails) to prove iptables sees bridged frames; cleanup with `sudo iptables -D FORWARD -i br0 -j DROP` and `sudo modprobe -r br_netfilter`.

verification.reasoning: Line 157 tells the reader to enable br_netfilter and 'add an iptables DROP rule on the bridge', then gives cleanup `sudo iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT` 'to ensure you don't lose connectivity'. That cleanup is genuinely broken: `-P FORWARD ACCEPT` only changes the chain's DEFAULT policy, which is consulted only after no rule matches. An appended `-A FORWARD ... -j DROP` rule still matches first, so the cleanup does NOT remove the drop and does NOT restore connectivity — directly contradicting the stated purpose. That is a real correctness flaw, not merely loose pedagogy. The other complaints (no concrete rule string, no observation step) are softer because this is the intentionally open-ended 'What to break' section whose other bullets are equally exploratory, but the mismatched/ineffective cleanup justifies the finding. Note the auditor's own fix uses `-i br0`, which is not the most reliable matcher for intra-bridge forwarded frames under br_netfilter (physdev semantics); an unqualified FORWARD DROP is cleaner for the demo. The verifiable point is that cleanup must delete the exact rule with `-D`, not reset the policy.
verification.refinedFix: Make the experiment concrete and self-undoing. Setup: `sudo modprobe br_netfilter` (this defaults net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1, which is what routes bridged frames through iptables). Break: `sudo iptables -A FORWARD -j DROP`, then show it bites with `sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c2 -W1 10.0.0.2` (now fails, proving iptables sees bridged frames). Cleanup MUST delete the exact rule, not reset policy: `sudo iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` (and optionally `sudo modprobe -r br_netfilter`). findings.problem: The underlay topology cannot carry traffic, so `ping -c 2 10.100.0.2` (and everything that depends on it) fails. Two separate veth pairs are created: vethA<->vethA_p and vethB<->vethB_p. The host-side ends vethA (192.168.99.10/24) and vethB (192.168.99.20/24) sit in init_net but are NOT bridged together — they are two distinct L2 segments. Namespace A treats 192.168.99.2 as on-link (same /24) and ARPs for it; the ARP request reaches vethA in init_net, where nobody owns .2 and ARP is not forwarded to vethB. So the VXLAN outer packet 192.168.99.1->192.168.99.2 never reaches namespace B. There is no bridge, no `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`, and no proxy_arp — none of the prerequisites that even a routed variant would need are stated. The entire chapter's experiment (encapsulated tcpdump, MTU break) rests on this ping working.
findings.evidence: sudo ip addr add 192.168.99.10/24 dev vethA / sudo ip addr add 192.168.99.20/24 dev vethB  (two unbridged veth pairs, both host ends on the same /24, no bridge/forwarding) ... sudo ip netns exec A ping -c 2 10.100.0.2
findings.suggestedFix: Give the two host-side veths a shared L2 underlay via a bridge instead of separate IP'd segments. Replace the `# Underlay veth pairs` block with: create the pairs, then `sudo ip link add br-underlay type bridge; sudo ip link set vethA master br-underlay; sudo ip link set vethB master br-underlay; sudo ip link set vethA up; sudo ip link set vethB up; sudo ip link set br-underlay up` and drop the 192.168.99.10/.20 addresses from vethA/vethB (the underlay addresses now live only on vethA_p=192.168.99.1 and vethB_p=192.168.99.2 inside the namespaces). Then add an explicit underlay sanity check before building the tunnel: `sudo ip netns exec A ping -c1 192.168.99.2  # underlay must work first`.

verification.reasoning: The lab (lines 93-124) builds two independent veth pairs (vethA<->vethA_p into netns A, vethB<->vethB_p into netns B) whose host-side ends sit in init_net as two separate L2 segments with no bridge between them. The VXLAN outer packet 192.168.99.1->192.168.99.2 is treated as on-link by namespace A (both ends share 192.168.99.0/24), so A ARPs for 192.168.99.2; that ARP exits on vethA into init_net where nobody owns .2, proxy_arp is off, and the request is never delivered to the vethB segment. The underlay therefore cannot carry the encapsulated traffic, so `ping -c 2 10.100.0.2` fails, and with it the encapsulated-tcpdump observation (line 128) and the entire MTU-break experiment (lines 133-146). Putting both host ends (.10/.20) on the same /24 in init_net is itself a misconfiguration that does not bridge or route between the two segments. This is not a bpftrace/CLI syntax issue and not an environment-only quirk — it is a structurally broken topology, correctly flagged as critical.

  sudo ip link add vethB type veth peer name vethB_p

findings.section: Set up a VXLAN tunnel (lab) — watch the encapsulated traffic
findings.problem: The capture is started AFTER the only traffic generator has already finished. Line 123 runs `ping -c 2 10.100.0.2`, which sends exactly two pings and exits. Only then (line 128) does the text say 'watch the encapsulated traffic' with a foreground tcpdump. By the time tcpdump is attached there is no VXLAN traffic flowing, so the reader sees an empty capture — directly contradicting 'You'll see UDP packets carrying the VXLAN-wrapped pings.' This violates the day01 rule that a capture must have a concurrent trigger (cf. day01 Obs2 starting tcpdump before the clones fire). The tcpdump also has no `-c` count or timeout, so it runs forever with no stated way to stop.
findings.evidence: sudo ip netns exec A ping -c 2 10.100.0.2   ...then later...   sudo tcpdump -i vethA -nn 'udp port 4789'   ("Then watch the encapsulated traffic")
findings.suggestedFix: Start the capture first (or in a second terminal) and generate traffic while it runs: `sudo timeout 5 tcpdump -i vethA -nn 'udp port 4789' &` then `sudo ip netns exec A ping -c 5 10.100.0.2`. Add the expected line: 'Each ICMP echo/reply appears as a UDP datagram to port 4789 between 192.168.99.1 and 192.168.99.2 — the VXLAN-encapsulated ping.' (If on the bridge fix from f1, `-i br-underlay` also works.)

verification.reasoning: Confirmed from the file. Line 123 runs `ping -c 2 10.100.0.2` and the code block closes at line 124. The tcpdump (line 128) is in a separate block introduced by 'Then watch the encapsulated traffic' — i.e. started AFTER the only traffic generator has already exited. tcpdump has no `-c` and no `timeout`, so it runs forever and shows nothing, directly contradicting line 131 ('You'll see UDP packets carrying the VXLAN-wrapped pings'). This is a structural missing-concurrent-trigger defect, the same class the day01 rule guards against — not an environment-only non-firing probe. Topology supports the capture interface: vethA (192.168.99.10, host) is the veth peer of vethA_p in netns A which holds the VXLAN local 192.168.99.1, so encapsulated UDP 192.168.99.1→.2 on port 4789 does traverse vethA. The suggested fix (capture first, generate traffic while it runs) is correct; it should add a brief startup delay so the backgrounded tcpdump attaches before ping fires.

sleep 1
sudo ip netns exec A ping -c 5 10.100.0.2
wait

Then add the expected line: "Each ICMP echo/reply appears as a UDP datagram to port 4789 between 192.168.99.1 and 192.168.99.2 — the VXLAN-encapsulated ping." (If the f1 bridge fix is applied, `-i br-underlay` also works.)

Two distinct flaws confirmed: (1) ordering -> no ICMP pings visible; (2) unbounded foreground tcpdump -> hangs. Audit's fix (capture first + sleep + bounded timeout + ping -c 5 + wait) reproduces the promised output cleanly. Fix is correct as written.

findings.problem: The 'break' likely does not break, because the VXLAN device is created with the default `df unset`. With the outer IP DF bit cleared, the 1550-byte outer packet (1500-byte inner + 50 VXLAN overhead) is simply IP-fragmented on the 1500-MTU underlay and reassembled at the far end — so the ping SUCCEEDS and the reader observes no failure, defeating the lesson. The comment 'Likely fails. Verify: tcpdump shows ICMP "frag needed" or just silent drop' is therefore unreliable and gives no concrete expected output. To make oversize packets actually fail (and trigger PMTUD / a drop, which is the whole point of the section), the tunnel must carry the DF bit on the outer header.
findings.evidence: sudo ip netns exec A ping -M do -s 1472 -c 2 10.100.0.2   # don't fragment, 1500 total\n# Likely fails. Verify: tcpdump shows ICMP "frag needed" or just silent drop.
findings.suggestedFix: Create the VXLAN with `df set` so the outer header refuses fragmentation: append `df set` to the `ip link add ... type vxlan` commands in the lab (e.g. `... remote 192.168.99.2 dstport 4789 df set`). Then state the deterministic expected result: 'With df set, the 1550-byte outer packet exceeds the 1500-byte underlay MTU and cannot be fragmented, so the send fails — `ping` reports 100% loss and you see no `udp port 4789` packets in tcpdump (or an ICMP "frag needed"). Drop vxlan0 back to MTU 1450 and the same ping succeeds.' If the author wants to keep df unset, change the prose to say the outer packet gets fragmented and the ping still works, illustrating the silent fragmentation cost rather than a failure.

verification.reasoning: Runtime-verified on the test VM (kernel 7.0.0-azure, vxlan_core.c). The finding's TARGET defect is real: the comment "Likely fails. Verify: tcpdump shows ICMP 'frag needed' or just silent drop" is inaccurate and gives no concrete expected output. There is NO on-wire ICMP frag-needed and it is NOT a silent drop. However, the finding's REASONING/premise is wrong: the break does NOT silently succeed. VXLAN calls skb_tunnel_check_pmtu() (vxlan_core.c:2514) unconditionally — independent of the df bit, with reply=false for a plain (non-bridge-port) vxlan0. It lowers the INNER route PMTU to 1450 without emitting any ICMP, so the kernel rejects the oversize DF packet locally with EMSGSIZE. Observed with default df-unset: seq=1 succeeds (outer DF clear, underlay IP-fragments the 1550B packet and the peer reassembles), then seq=2,3 print "ping: sendmsg: Message too long" => 66% loss. With "df set": clean 100% loss, every packet "ping: sendmsg: Message too long". So the finding's claim that df-unset means the ping fully succeeds with no observable failure is empirically false (only the first packet sneaks through). The fix (add df set) is a reasonable improvement that yields deterministic 100% loss, but the finding's proposed expected-output prose ("no udp port 4789 packets / ICMP frag needed") is also inaccurate and must be corrected. Separately (outside this finding's 135-146 range): the lab setup never bridges the two host-side veths, so the underlay has no path and even the baseline overlay ping gets 100% loss — I had to add a bridge to test at all; that is a distinct, more fundamental bug worth its own finding.
verification.refinedFix: Replace the unreliable comment with the actual, runtime-verified failure mode. The oversize ping fails with a LOCAL kernel error, not an on-wire ICMP and not a silent drop. Document expected output (default df unset): seq=1 succeeds ("1480 bytes from 10.100.0.2"), then "ping: sendmsg: Message too long" twice, ending "3 packets transmitted, 1 received, +2 errors, 66% packet loss". Explain why: at MTU 1500 the inner 1500-byte frame plus ~50B overhead would make a 1550-byte outer packet. The kernel's tunnel PMTU check (skb_tunnel_check_pmtu in vxlan_core.c) lowers the INNER route PMTU to 1450; the first DF packet still slips out (outer DF is clear by default, so the 1500-MTU underlay IP-fragments it and the peer reassembles), but every subsequent DF packet is rejected locally as "Message too long" (EMSGSIZE). It is NOT an on-wire ICMP "fragmentation needed" and NOT a silent drop — drop that wording. Optionally append `df set` to the netns-A `ip link add ... type vxlan` line to make it deterministic — then ALL packets fail (100% loss, every line "ping: sendmsg: Message too long"). Do NOT adopt the finding's "no udp port 4789 packets / ICMP frag needed" phrasing; it does not match observed behavior. Prerequisite (separate fix in the setup block, lines ~93-124): the two host-side veths must be enslaved to a bridge in init_net, otherwise the underlay has no path and even the baseline overlay ping fails 100% — the experiment cannot be observed without it.

With the default `df unset` VXLAN, the kernel's tunnel PMTU check (skb_tunnel_check_pmtu) lowers the inner route PMTU to 1450, so a 1500-byte DF inner packet is rejected locally at sendmsg with EMSGSIZE rather than being fragmented, dropped silently, or eliciting an on-wire ICMP frag-needed — contradicting the book's "tcpdump shows ICMP 'frag needed' or just silent drop." Minor caveat: the audit's fix prose quotes "-c 3 ... +2 errors, 66% packet loss"; the book command is actually `-c 2`, which yields "+1 errors, 50% packet loss". The failure MODE described by the fix is correct; only the packet count in the fix's sample output should match the book's `-c 2` (or change the book to `-c 3`). Also note: first packet succeeds because the lowered inner PMTU/route cache isn't yet established on the very first probe; subsequent sends hit the cached 1450 PMTU and fail.

findings.section: Set up a VXLAN tunnel (lab) / Today's experiment
findings.problem: No teardown is provided. The lab creates namespaces A and B, host-side veths vethA/vethB (and, with the f1 fix, a bridge) that all persist in init_net after the chapter ends. Deleting a netns auto-removes the in-netns peer, but vethA/vethB live in init_net and survive, leaving stale interfaces and addresses on 192.168.99.0/24 that will collide if the reader re-runs the lab. The MTU experiment restores vxlan0 MTU (good), but the overall lab has no cleanup, unlike day01 which always stops/removes what it started.
findings.evidence: Lab ends at line 124 (`ping`) / experiment ends at line 146 (`mtu 1450`); no `ip netns del` / `ip link del` anywhere in the chapter.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a cleanup block at the end of the experiment: `sudo ip netns del A` / `sudo ip netns del B` / `sudo ip link del vethA` / `sudo ip link del vethB` (and `sudo ip link del br-underlay` if the bridge fix is applied). Note that deleting the namespaces removes vethA_p/vethB_p and vxlan0 automatically; the host-side veths and bridge must be deleted explicitly.

verification.reasoning: Verified against day12.md: the lab (lines 93-124) creates netns A/B, veth pairs vethA/vethA_p and vethB/vethB_p, and vxlan0 inside each netns; the experiment ends at line 146 restoring vxlan0 MTU. There is genuinely no `ip netns del`/`ip link del` anywhere in the chapter, so the core 'no teardown provided' complaint is accurate, and re-running the lab will collide (`ip netns add A` -> 'File exists'), inconsistent with day01's clean teardown. That makes adding a cleanup block a legitimate fix. BUT the finding's mechanism is wrong: it claims host-side vethA/vethB survive `ip netns del`. They do not. veth pairs delete symmetrically, and on netns teardown virtual devices with dellink ops (veth_dellink) are unregistered, not moved to init_net. So `ip netns del A` deletes vethA_p which auto-deletes its peer vethA; same for B. The suggested explicit `ip link del vethA`/`ip link del vethB` are redundant and would error ('Cannot find device') if run after the namespaces are deleted. Only the bridge from the f1 fix lives independently in init_net and needs explicit deletion. Confirming the missing-cleanup defect but correcting the fix.

Deleting the two namespaces is sufficient to remove everything created inside them AND the host-side veths (veth pairs are deleted symmetrically; netns teardown unregisters the in-netns veth, which removes its init_net peer too): `sudo ip netns del A` / `sudo ip netns del B`. Do NOT add `sudo ip link del vethA` / `sudo ip link del vethB` — those devices are already gone and the commands will error. Only if the f1 bridge fix is applied, also add `sudo ip link del br-underlay` (the bridge lives in init_net and is not removed by deleting the namespaces). Optionally make it idempotent with `2>/dev/null || true`.

findings.problem: The tcp_set_state probe prints args->state, which is a raw integer (TCP_ESTABLISHED=1, TCP_SYN_SENT=2, TCP_CLOSE=7, TCP_CLOSE_WAIT=8, TCP_LAST_ACK=9, etc.). The reader's actual output is lines like 'set_state 0xffff... -> 2', but the prose at line 150 describes the trace in SYMBOLIC names ('SYN_SENT -> ESTABLISHED -> CLOSE_WAIT -> LAST_ACK -> CLOSED'). No mapping from the printed numbers to the named states is given, so the reader cannot connect what they see to what the prose claims. Two distinct sk pointers (server listener vs client) are also interleaved with no way to tell them apart.
findings.evidence: fentry:tcp_set_state { printf("set_state %p -> %d\n", args->sk, args->state); }  ...  You'll see init → get_port (server) → init (client) → connect → set_state through SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED.

findings.problem: The trigger connects to 'localhost', which on a default Linux box resolves to BOTH 127.0.0.1 and ::1 (confirmed in /etc/hosts). glibc/most clients prefer IPv6, so nc frequently connects over ::1. In that case the kernel takes the tcp_v6_connect path and the headline 'fentry:tcp_v4_connect' probe NEVER fires — the reader sees init/get_port/set_state lines but no 'connect %p' line, silently breaking the central part of the lifecycle demo. The server 'nc -l 9999' may also bind IPv6-only on some systems, causing the connect to fail outright.

findings.suggestedFix: Force IPv4 on both sides so tcp_v4_connect is guaranteed to fire: `nc -l 127.0.0.1 9999 &` and `echo hi | nc -q 1 127.0.0.1 9999`. Optionally add a note: 'We use 127.0.0.1 (not localhost) so the connection goes over IPv4 and tcp_v4_connect fires; localhost may resolve to ::1 and take the tcp_v6_connect path.'

verification.reasoning: Lines 139/145 confirm the mismatch: the headline probe is exactly `fentry:tcp_v4_connect`, but the trigger dials `localhost`. On a default Linux box /etc/hosts maps `localhost` to both 127.0.0.1 and ::1, and getaddrinfo (glibc, RFC 3484) returns ::1 first, so most nc builds connect over IPv6 — taking the tcp_v6_connect path and never firing the `connect %p` line. That line is the centerpiece of the lifecycle demo promised on line 150 (init -> get_port -> init -> connect -> set_state...), so a reader can silently lose the most important output. This is NOT the environment-only non-firing quirk called out in the nuance (tcp_v4_connect fires fine for IPv4 traffic); it's a genuine trigger defect — the command simply drives the wrong protocol. The fix is deterministic and harmless: forcing 127.0.0.1 guarantees the IPv4 path. The bpftrace script itself (args-> usage, %p, no exit) is clean, so no other bug-pattern violation applies.

Pin both endpoints to IPv4 so tcp_v4_connect is guaranteed to fire:

```bash

```

Add a one-line note: "We use 127.0.0.1, not `localhost` — `localhost` resolves to both 127.0.0.1 and ::1, and most clients prefer ::1, which would take the `tcp_v6_connect` path and never fire our `tcp_v4_connect` probe." The audit's worry is only valid on systems whose /etc/hosts genuinely aliases localhost to ::1 (and a v6 listener exists) — not the common case and not this VM. The suggested fix (pin 127.0.0.1) is harmless and slightly more robust, so it's a reasonable defensive note, but the original is NOT broken. (Note: `getent hosts localhost` — the single-family legacy path — did return ::1, but that path is not what nc/getaddrinfo uses, and the empirical connect went over IPv4.)

findings.problem: With BSD/OpenBSD nc, an unconnected `nc -ul 9999` connect()s to the first peer's source address on the first datagram; the second `echo | nc` uses a different ephemeral source port, so the second datagram fails the connected-socket 4-tuple match and is not delivered to that socket. The reader may then NOT see the second 'queue to sk=' line, contradicting 'one send -> one rcv -> one queue per datagram'. This nc quirk is exactly the connected-vs-unconnected lookup the chapter teaches, but it is unexplained and undermines reproducibility.
findings.evidence: echo "hello" | nc -u 127.0.0.1 9999 / echo "world" | nc -u 127.0.0.1 9999  (two separate client invocations, two source ports)
findings.suggestedFix: Send both datagrams from one client process so the source port is stable, e.g. `printf 'hello\nworld\n' | nc -u -q1 127.0.0.1 9999`, OR add a sentence: 'nc's server connects to the first sender, so a second datagram from a new source port is dropped by the 4-tuple lookup (__udp4_lib_lookup) — exactly the connected-UDP behavior described above.'

verification.reasoning: Real for OpenBSD netcat (default `nc` on Debian/Ubuntu). In UDP listen mode it MSG_PEEKs the first datagram then connect()s back to that sender's (addr,port); the socket is then matched only by the full 4-tuple, and compute_score() in __udp4_lib_lookup rejects any datagram whose source port != sk_dport. The two separate `echo | nc` clients use different ephemeral source ports, so the second datagram triggers udp_rcv but NOT __udp_queue_rcv_skb — the reader sees the second 'queue to sk=' line missing, contradicting the stated 'one send -> one rcv -> one queue per datagram.' This is exactly the connected-UDP lookup the chapter teaches (it even cites __udp4_lib_lookup and '4-tuple for connected UDP'), but it is left unexplained. Confidence is medium, not high, because: (a) netcat-traditional/busybox nc stay unconnected and both datagrams would queue, so it bites only on OpenBSD nc; and (b) the suggested fix's first variant `printf 'hello\nworld\n' | nc` is itself buggy — one pipe read becomes one sendto (one datagram), so it would not show two datagrams. The explanatory-sentence variant is correct.
verification.refinedFix: Preferred: add one sentence after line 102 explaining the quirk: "If your `nc` is the OpenBSD variant, the listener connect()s to the first sender after the first datagram, so the second `echo | nc` (a new process with a fresh ephemeral source port) fails the 4-tuple match in __udp4_lib_lookup and is dropped — you'll see its `recv` but no `queue` line. That IS the connected-UDP behavior described above." Optionally, to keep two datagrams while making the source port stable, drive both writes from a single client process/socket with a gap: `{ echo hello; sleep 1; echo world; } | nc -u -q1 127.0.0.1 9999`. Do NOT use `printf 'hello\nworld\n' | nc` — a single pipe read collapses into one sendto/one datagram, so it would not demonstrate two datagrams.

findings.vmNotes: The defect is real and reproduces cleanly on the VM's OpenBSD nc. After the first datagram the unconnected listener effectively binds to the first peer's 4-tuple, so the second `echo | nc` (new process, fresh ephemeral source port) fails the connected-socket match in __udp4_lib_lookup and is delivered to a different socket, not the listener. The reader sees a recv with no matching queue line for the second datagram, contradicting line 102's "one send -> one rcv -> one queue per datagram." The audit's preferred fix (a sentence explaining the connected-UDP quirk) and its alternative (single-process client with a gap to keep the source port stable) both hold up — the single-client variant delivered both datagrams. Two caveats the audit understated: (1) the chapter's own bpftrace probe `fentry:__udp_queue_rcv_skb` does not exist on Linux 7.0 (it's `__udp_enqueue_schedule_skb` / `udp_queue_rcv_one_skb`), so the trace command would itself fail to attach as written — a separate, compounding bug worth a fix; (2) the listener must be a long-lived `nc -ul` for the quirk to bite (it does in the book's example). I avoided port 9999 because other parallel agents had a leftover listener there; used 5399x ports instead, which does not change the result.
